name: PT Bank Kasikorn Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: KBank Indonesia: a premium multiple on a bank still to earn its cost of equity
frontmatter.summary: BMAS trades at a large premium to book while earning a fraction of its cost of equity, because nearly nine tenths of the shares are held by Kasikornbank and barely a tenth trades. On management's own plan - a loan book more than doubling by 2030 - the bank still earns a low-single-digit return on equity at the end of the decade. Fundamental value is a fraction of the price; we rate SELL.
thesis: The franchise is being built, not yet earning: the loan book doubled in three years and management targets more than double it again by 2030, but the FY2025 return on equity was a fraction of one per cent and the nine months to September 2026 produced a loss.

The build is funded by the parent, not by deposits: borrowings rose several-fold during 2026 under a bilateral facility from Kasikornbank, which is why the margin is compressing rather than widening with scale.
The rights issue is priced below the market and at about book: the controlling shareholder itself does not pay the multiple the market pays for this franchise.
Fundamental value of Rp60 per share against a Rp406 price. Our target is Rp249, the probability-weighted blend of three concentrated-ownership regime outcomes, -38.7%.
The free float is below the exchange minimum; the name sits on the high-shareholding-concentration list and out of the IHSG, and the rights issue makes the concentration worse.

catalysts.event: Cum-rights and recording date for PMHMETD IV
Rights issue settlement; enlarged paid-up capital
First free-float deadline under the exchange rule
FY2026 audited results - first full year at the new loan scale

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp249 (-38.7%).** The case is not complicated. PT Bank Kasikorn Indonesia Tbk - Bank Maspion until the name change in August 2026 [S8] - is a small commercial bank [S2] controlled by Kasikornbank of Thailand, which holds 89.5% of it through Kasikorn Vision Financial [S6]. It trades at 1.13x book on the shares in issue today, while earning 0.5% on equity, and it lost money in the nine months to September 2026 [S9].

Our fundamental value is Rp60 per share against the Rp406 close in our market data [S0]; the exchange registry carries Rp380 for the same session [S12], and the valuation section reconciles the two and uses the registered data pack, the only price our model can pair with a matching share count and turnover. The target of Rp249 is not the fundamental value: because this is a concentrated-ownership name, the house lens rules that only part of the premium to fundamental value closes within twelve months, and the target is the probability-weighted blend of three regime outcomes - the base regime alone is worth Rp202. The mechanism is set out in the valuation section. We still rate SELL, because even a partial closing of a gap that wide is a large negative return.

Three things move the value. First, the margin: net interest income on assets fell over the nine months to September 2026 [S9] as parent borrowings at a US dollar reference rate plus a margin [S6] replaced cheap deposits, with the CASA ratio at 27.2% [S2]. Second, the cost base: BOPO fell from 120.1% to 97.2% in FY2025 [S2], and whether it keeps falling as the loan book doubles is the whole bull case. Third, the capital: the rights issue [S5] buys roughly two years of growth at the current pace, and the controlling shareholder takes all of it - which tells you both that the group supports the bank and that it does not expect a dividend.

In the Indonesian banking market a bank of this size is a price-taker on funding: it cannot set
deposit rates, it borrows wholesale or from its parent, and its cost-to-income ratio only falls when
the loan book grows into a fixed cost base. That is the phase this bank is in, and it is why a plan
that doubles the book can still leave the return on equity in single digits for years.

KBank Indonesia is a commercial bank headquartered in Surabaya, offering savings, current accounts, time deposits, credit, trade finance, foreign exchange, QRIS and transaction banking to corporate, small-business and retail customers [S2][S8]. It is the Indonesian arm of Kasikornbank PCL, one of the ten largest banks in ASEAN by assets, and its stated strategy is to connect Indonesian corporate and state-owned borrowers to KBank's cross-border network in Thailand, China, Vietnam and other regional markets [S7][S8]. The name change from Bank Maspion to KBank Indonesia was completed in August 2026 after approval by the financial services authority, and the company presents it as the end of a three-year transformation rather than a rebrand [S8].

The business is essentially one product: corporate credit. The loan book grew from IDR8.78tn in FY2022 to IDR17.34tn in FY2025 [S2], and management says corporate lending remains the growth engine into 2026, targeting large companies and state-owned enterprises using the regional network [S2]. Fee businesses - trade finance, foreign exchange, QRIS, transaction banking - are being built but are small: other operating income was IDR74.8bn against IDR711.2bn of net interest income in FY2025 [S0]. That mix is the reason the franchise has little fee ballast when the margin turns, and why the bank's profitability is essentially a spread business with a thin cost base.

Scale and position. With IDR22.40tn of assets [S2] the bank sits well below the size threshold at which Indonesian banks are treated as systemically significant, and management has spoken of reaching that tier [S7]. Its share of Indonesian banking assets is a fraction of a per cent. It is a challenger with a wealthy parent, not a franchise with pricing power. The moat, such as it is, is the parent: funding lines [S6], a Fitch national long-term rating of AA+(idn) with a stable outlook, upgraded in July 2026 on the strength of that relationship [S7], and access to Thai and regional corporate clients a standalone bank of this size could not win. Against that, the parent relationship is also the concentration: the same counterparty sets the funding price, supplies the capital and owns the strategy.

Distribution and people. The bank is a relationship-lending institution rather than a branch network: it employs 771 people [S0], which at this balance sheet size means a small corporate coverage team and a digital retail offer rather than a mass-market branch franchise. That is the right cost structure for the strategy, and also why the deposit franchise is weak: without branches, CASA has to be won through transaction banking, which takes years.

Ownership. Kasikorn Vision Financial Pte Ltd holds 86.0% directly and the KBank group 89.5% [S6]. The free float is 10.6% [S12] and institutions hold 2.5% [S0]. The public shareholders are, in practice, a residual.

Indonesian banking is a market of large, well-capitalised incumbents and a long tail of sub-scale
banks. System loan growth has run in the high single digits and the policy rate has been held at a
level that keeps funding costs elevated for everyone. For a small bank the consequence is
straightforward: deposit competition is brutal, CASA is hard to win without a transaction-banking
franchise, and the marginal funding source is the wholesale or shareholder line.

That is what this balance sheet shows. Third-party deposits fell to IDR10,010.0bn at September 2026 while loans reached IDR21,550.0bn [S9], and the gap was funded by a bilateral facility from Kasikornbank at a US dollar reference rate plus a margin, with most of the committed amount drawn by late October [S6]. A bank that funds incremental assets in dollars against rupiah loans is choosing growth over margin, and the nine-month figures show the price: net interest income of IDR549.6bn grew a fraction as fast as assets [S9]. It has also imported an FX line into the profit and loss that a deposit-funded bank does not carry: the nine months to September 2026 carried a loss on the foreign-exchange translation line reported at IDR267.7bn [S9], large enough to turn a growing net interest income into a loss at the pre-tax level [S9].

Regulation. Two rules matter more than the banking rules here. The exchange's minimum free-float requirement, phased in with an intermediate step, leaves this bank below the threshold at 10.6% [S11][S12], and the rights issue about to complete increases the controller's share rather than reducing it [S5]. Separately, the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, on which the stock appears as of 22 October 2026 [S10], took HSC names out of the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S13]. Neither changes the banking business; both change who can own the stock, and therefore what the marginal buyer will pay.

Competitive position and five forces. Supplier power - depositors and the parent - is high and rising, because neither needs this bank. Buyer power is high: large corporates and state-owned enterprises price every bank against every other, and a bank with a single-product balance sheet and a funding cost above the system's cannot win on price. The threat of new entrants is low for banking licences but high for the specific corporate segment, where foreign banks and the large domestic groups compete for the same mandates. Substitutes - capital markets and multifinance - are real for the best corporate names. Rivalry is intense, which is why a bank that reports a wide margin in one year cannot hold it in the next. The one genuine advantage is the parent's network and balance sheet [S7], and it is worth something: it brings regional corporate clients and a funding line that no standalone bank of this size could obtain [S6]. It is not worth the current multiple on today's returns.

Growth and the cycle. Indonesian corporate credit growth has been supported by commodity-related
investment and by state spending, and the house macro view is that the rupiah stays under pressure
with the policy rate held. For a dollar-funded lender that is the wrong combination: the asset yield
does not rise with the funding cost. This is the external influence that matters most to the
forecast, more than any change in the banking rulebook.

**History.** Net interest income was IDR711.2bn in FY2025 on IDR22,400.0bn of earning assets [S0], a margin on assets of just over three per cent. The FY2024 loss of IDR-247.2bn came from a cost base that exceeded operating income - BOPO of 120.1% [S2][S0] - and from an impairment charge on a much smaller book. FY2025's IDR31.8bn profit was a recovery year: gross NPL fell from 3.26% to 2.26% [S2], so provisions were released rather than charged, and BOPO fell to 97.2% [S2]. A profit that depends on write-backs is not a run-rate, and we do not model one.

**The 2026 turn.** The nine months to September 2026 produced a net loss of IDR5.8bn, reversing a profit of the same period a year earlier [S9]. Net interest income still rose to IDR549.6bn as the loan book reached IDR21,550.0bn, but interest expense of IDR588.8bn and other operating expenses of IDR549.4bn consumed almost all of it, and BOPO rose to 100.0% [S9]. Deposits fell to IDR10,010.0bn against loans of IDR21,550.0bn [S9]: the bank grew by close to a third in nine months and funded it with the parent's money rather than with deposits, which is why the margin compressed while the book grew.

**The fourth-quarter bridge.** We do not forecast a rebound we cannot source. [S9] reports the loss on the foreign-exchange translation line at IDR267.7bn for the nine months and gives no quarterly split of it and no statement that it reverses in the fourth quarter. Carrying the nine-month run-rate into Q4 is therefore the only quarterly bridge the evidence supports, and on that bridge FY2026E is a small full-year loss of IDR-5.8bn against the IDR31.8bn of FY2025 - the pivot year stays negative, and the three valuation methods absorb it rather than a sign flip resting on an unsourced assumption. We reproduce the rest of the arithmetic at the nine-month level: opex at the run-rate, a near-nil credit charge, and the margin where the parent's dollar funding puts it [S9][S6].

**Forecast.** We model loan growth of 30.0% in FY2026E, then a decelerating path to the long-run rate, reaching IDR40,800.3bn in FY2030E - the company's own target of more than IDR40.00tn [S7], not a haircut to it. Deposits grow several points slower throughout, so the parent line stays part of the funding plan rather than being assumed away. The margin is 3.1% in FY2026E and recovers only gradually to 3.4% by FY2030E, below the FY2025 level: the rights-issue cash and a rebuilt deposit base help, but we do not assume a re-rating of the funding mix that the CASA trend does not support [S2].

Cost-to-income falls from 96.0% to 68.5% as income nearly triples against a cost base growing with inflation. That is the assumption the whole bull case rests on, and it is also the one the company has been delivering: BOPO fell by more than twenty points in a single year [S2]. Credit cost is 0.1% in FY2026E - above the FY2025 write-back and below the FY2024 charge - then 1.0% through the cycle. A book that has doubled in three years has not been tested by a downturn, but we do not add a caution overlay the evidence does not support; the through-cycle number already sits above what the bank has actually booked in the last two years.

On those inputs the bank earns IDR83.7bn in FY2030E on IDR6,435.8bn of equity, a 1.3% return on equity [S0]. That is the result that matters: after five years of executing its own plan the franchise is barely profitable, and it takes the whole forecast horizon to reach even a low-single-digit return - 3.9% by FY2035E - against a cost of equity of 11.9%. The equity base barely grows because the profits are small, and the share count grows because the rights issue adds stock [S5] - so book value per share rises slowly even as the loan book multiplies.

**Capital and liquidity.** The CAR of 45.8% at FY2025 [S2] is the strongest thing about this bank and it is being spent: risk-weighted assets grow with the book, and the rights issue at Rp350 per share for IDR1.01tn [S5] is the capital that keeps the ratio above the regulatory floor. We model no dividend until the long-run years and a payout of 15.0% by FY2030E, because a bank growing loans at double digits on a single-digit return on equity has nothing to spare [S0].

**Earnings quality.** Three flags, all optics-class rather than manipulation-class. FY2025 profit was flattered by a provision write-back as NPL fell [S2]. Non-interest income is volatile and the foreign-exchange translation line swung to a large reported loss in the nine months to September 2026 [S9]. And the assets are funded with dollar debt [S6] against a rupiah loan book, which puts an FX line through the profit and loss that a deposit-funded bank does not carry; the nine-month loss on that line is the evidence [S9]. None of these suggests fabricated earnings; all three mean the headline profit is a poor guide to run-rate earnings, and we forecast the operating lines rather than extrapolating the reported result.

**Method.** A bank is valued on what its book earns, so the primary method is justified price to book, with residual income and a dividend discount model as cross-checks. Residual income is the same arithmetic in present-value form; the dividend model is a check, but with no dividend history [S0] and none modelled until the long-run years it adds little. That is why it prints Rp16 against Rp39 for the primary method, a gap of -58.7% that is a statement about dividend policy rather than about value. Residual income at Rp6 against Rp39 for the primary method is the more useful divergence: it is lower because the early years earn almost nothing, and because the base case now carries real losses in FY2027E-FY2029E as the credit charge normalises to the through-cycle level against a cost base that does not fall [S9][S2]. We keep the house weights of half the primary method, three tenths residual income and two tenths dividend model; the primary method is the one that takes the long-run return seriously rather than the near-term one.
**The build.**

Cost of equity is 11.9%: a long-dated rupiah sovereign yield, the house equity-risk premium and a country premium, with beta at the configuration default for banks because no banking regression set exists. There is no debt in the discount rate - a bank's liabilities are its raw material, not a financing choice - and the calculation is in rupiah at rupiah rates, per the house banks card.

The sustainable return on equity is built from the card's own components rather than asserted. At the terminal inputs of the model - a margin of 3.4% on average earning assets, leverage measured as average earning assets over average equity, cost-to-income of 62.0% and the 1.0% through-cycle credit charge, with non-interest income a fraction of a point and the modelled tax rate [S0][S9] - the arithmetic lands on 3.95%, which is the same number the engine prints for FY2035E, 3.95%. An earlier draft of this report carried a higher figure here while calling it the terminal return; that was wrong on its own arithmetic - the higher number would need a cost-to-income near the mid fifties or leverage well above what the balance sheet shows - and it is withdrawn. The multiple method and the residual-income terminal value now use one number, so they cannot disagree. Terminal growth is 3.0%, inside the banks-card bound that growth cannot exceed the return on equity times the retention ratio: a return this far below the cost of equity cannot support more.

Warranted price to book is 0.11x against a traded 1.13x. The traded multiple is price over book value per share on the shares in issue today. We do not quote a forward multiple as the traded one because the bank template raises the share count for the rights issue without adding the proceeds to equity [S5], so the engine's forward book value per share falls mechanically rather than economically. The reason the warranted multiple sits so far below book is arithmetic, not sentiment: when the return on equity is below the cost of equity, growth destroys value and the warranted multiple falls below book, the more so the faster the book grows.

**The two prices.** The model prices the stock at Rp406, the 9 November 2026 close in the registered data pack, which is the only price the archive lets us pair with a matching share count, market capitalisation and turnover [S0]. The exchange registry's own record for the same session carries Rp380 and a reported 1.06x price to book [S12]; the two same-date prices disagree and we cannot reconcile them from the sources we hold. We use the pack price throughout, so the traded multiple here is 1.13x and the expected return is -38.7%; measured from the registry close the same Rp249 target is a smaller negative return, and neither the rating nor the target changes.

**What the price implies.** At Rp406 the market capitalises 1.13x a book that earns 3.9% only at the end of the forecast horizon. Reverse-solving the model, the price requires a sustainable return on equity several points above what the plan delivers - roughly the return of a bank twice this size with a deposit franchise this one does not have. The alternative explanation is not fundamentals at all: with 10.6% of the shares trading [S12] and the KBank group holding 89.5% [S6], the marginal price is set by a thin float rather than by a valuation, and the liquidity discount the engine applies (20.0%) is the price of that.

We tested the strategic-buyer explanation and it does not hold on the evidence. A holder at 89.5% that has just lent USD341m and backstops the rights issue could buy the residual float, but the only price the controller has actually set recently is the rights price of Rp350 a share [S5] - below the market, and at about book - and the free-float rule forces it to release shares, not to buy them. A tender above standalone value would require a filing of which there is none; the post-balance-sheet search found the facility, the rights issue and the name change, nothing else [S5][S6][S8]. Control value is therefore stated as a scenario, not the base case.

**The no-growth alternative.** Because the base case grows the book at a return below the cost of equity, the value-destroying path is not the only one shareholders could own. At zero growth and full payout the same return is worth the return divided by the cost of equity applied to book value - well under half of book, but well above the engine's Rp60, which capitalises perpetual growth at a return below the cost of equity. We keep the growth path because the controller's own plan is a loan book above IDR40,000.0bn by 2030 [S7] and the rights proceeds are committed to it [S5]; the no-growth value is the bull variant, not the base case, and it is still below today's price.

**Funding and the deposit base.** Deposits are the missing leg of this franchise: they fell to IDR10,010.0bn at September 2026 while loans reached IDR21,550.0bn [S9], and the gap was funded by the parent facility at SOFR plus a margin [S6]. CASA was 27.16% at FY2025 [S2] and the company quotes no deposit beta; what is observable is a shrinking, expensive deposit base against the house BI path, so the mix enters the valuation through the NIM path rather than through a deposit line the bank template does not print. Of the September borrowings, about two thirds is the facility and the remainder is unexplained by any disclosure we could archive.

**The concentrated-ownership lens.** This is a konglo-regime name by the house definition: it is on the high-shareholding-concentration list as of 22 October 2026 [S10], out of the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S13], and its free float is 10.6% against the exchange minimum [S12][S11]. The engine computes the fundamental value first, as above, and then applies the regime step: the price sits at 7.6x fundamental value measured before the twelve-month roll-forward, and each of three regime outcomes closes a different share of that log gap over twelve months. In the base regime 40.0% of the gap closes and the rest is kept, which is worth Rp202 - that is the base-regime target, and it is not the number we publish. In the bear regime, where 80.0% of the gap closes, the value is Rp90; in the bull regime, where the gap does not close and even re-expands (-5.0%), it is Rp503. The Rp249 target is the probability-weighted blend of those three, at the house regime weights of a quarter, a half and a quarter, and it sits above the base regime because the bull outcome - a quarter of the weight, and a value above the current price - pulls it up. Stated plainly: the SELL does not depend on the bull. Even if the bull regime were weighted at fifteen per cent rather than a quarter, the target would fall back toward the base regime's Rp202, still far below the Rp406 price.

We did not bend a single fundamental input to reach the market price, and we did not shade them to pre-empt a fall. The lens exists because float-constrained prices persist: the controller holds almost nine tenths of the shares [S6], the rights issue adds shares the controller itself subscribes [S5], and nothing forces the gap to close on our calendar. It is still a negative expected return, and it is a SELL rather than a HOLD.
**Sensitivity.**

The valuation is most sensitive to the sustainable return on equity and the cost of equity: a point on the return moves warranted price to book by about a tenth of book, and a point on the cost of equity moves it about a tenth as much in the opposite direction, which is why the warranted multiple is so thin at this level of profitability. The credit-cost axis matters less than the margin and cost axes, because the earnings base is so thin that the cost ratio, not the provisioning rate, decides whether the bank earns anything at all.
**Risks, with likelihood and impact.**

items: *Funding and margin (high likelihood, high impact).* Growth is funded with dollar borrowings from
the parent at a reference rate plus a margin [S6]. A stronger dollar or higher US rates raises the
cost and the FX line together, and the first nine months of 2026 already produced a large
foreign-exchange translation loss on exactly that mechanism [S9].
*Credit quality (medium likelihood, high impact).* Gross NPL fell to 2.26% [S2] but the
book has doubled in three years and is concentrated in corporate and state-owned lending [S2]. One
large default is material at this size, and the provisioning buffer is thin relative to the book.
*Capital (medium likelihood, high impact).* Risk-weighted assets grow with the book; the rights
issue [S5] covers roughly two years at the current pace. Another call on the parent is likely if
growth continues, and each one dilutes public holders at a price the controller sets.
*Liquidity and free float (high likelihood, medium impact).* With 10.6% free
float [S12] and very thin turnover [S12], an institutional position cannot be built or exited. The
deadline is sized, not just named: if the public holders do not take up the 2.87bn new
shares at Rp350, the float falls to about nine per cent of the 20.97bn
post-rights count, and reaching the interim threshold needs roughly seven hundred million shares -
close to three hundred billion rupiah at the current price - released into turnover of about a
hundred and forty million rupiah a day, which is nearly two thousand trading days of volume. That
is the largest mechanical supply risk in the name and it is why the liquidity discount stays in the
valuation even after the regime adjustment. The engine
applies a liquidity discount for it, and the discount is not a technicality: it is the reason the
price can sit where it does.
*Regulatory (medium likelihood, medium impact).* The exchange's free-float rule with an
intermediate deadline in March 2027 [S11]. Non-compliance invites further index exclusion and could
force a controller selldown - good for the float in the long run, bad for the price when it
happens.
*Governance and related parties (high likelihood, medium impact).* A large bilateral facility from
the controlling shareholder is a related-party transaction by definition [S6]. It is disclosed and
priced off a market reference rate, but the bank's funding, capital and strategy are all set by one
counterparty, and public shareholders have no leverage over any of them.

blocks.text: **Scenarios.**

Bear (probability of three tenths): cost of credit rises as the young book seasons, the margin stays where the dollar funding cost puts it, growth slows as capital binds and cost-to-income improves more slowly; value falls. Base (just under half): the plan is executed - the loan book reaches the company's target, the margin recovers modestly and cost-to-income falls by double digits - and the bank still earns only 3.9% at the end of the forecast horizon, its best year in the plan. Bull (one quarter): the cost base stays flat in nominal terms, CASA is rebuilt, the margin settles at four per cent and credit cost stays below half a per cent, producing a low-teens return. The business shocks are mirrored across the same drivers, and the probabilities reflect what each path requires rather than a symmetric spread around a cautious centre. The dispersion of values is wide because a bank whose warranted multiple sits near zero is convex in the return: a path that lifts the return towards the cost of equity is worth several times the base case, and we weight that path at one quarter rather than treating it as the central one. Even with a quarter of it in the blend, the published target sits far below the market price - the bull is in the probability weight, not in the base case.

**Regime scenarios.** Separately, the lens carries three regime outcomes for how much of the premium to fundamental value survives twelve months: 80.0% of the log gap closes in the bear regime case, 40.0% in the base and -5.0% in the bull, producing regime values of Rp90, Rp202 and Rp503 at the house weights of a quarter, a half and a quarter - the blend behind our Rp249 target. The lens is not a view that the premium is deserved; it is the base case for how fast a float this thin can reprice. The dates that matter are the free-float step in March 2027 [S11], the final step in March 2028 [S11], and the index reviews in between [S13].

**What would change our view.** A deposit franchise: CASA rising materially above the current 27.2% [S2] with the margin stabilising near four per cent would make the end-decade return double-digit and the multiple defensible. A credible free-float selldown would remove the liquidity discount and could change the lens. A dividend - a signal that the group treats the bank as mature rather than as a growth platform - would change the weight of the dividend model in the method set. On the other side, a second loss year in a row would make the capital call more likely and the bear case the base case.

**Ownership and control.** Kasikorn Vision Financial holds 86.0% and the KBank group 89.5% [S6]; the free float is 10.6% on the IDX registry reading of 9 November 2026 [S12], with 2.5% held by institutions [S0]. The company is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list as of 22 October 2026 [S10], and HSC names were taken out of the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 [S13]. The exchange states in the same list that inclusion does not by itself show a breach of the capital-market rules [S10]; it is a disclosure status, not a finding of wrongdoing. The consequence is mechanical: index funds cannot own it, and the marginal buyer is retail.

**Free float.** At 10.6% [S12] the bank is below the exchange minimum, with an intermediate deadline of 12.5% in March 2027 and the full threshold in March 2028 [S11]. The rights issue, in which the controller takes up its full entitlement plus the shares the Thai parent would have taken [S5], increases concentration rather than reducing it: the new shares go mostly to the controller's vehicle. We see no mechanism for reaching the threshold before the deadline other than a controller selldown, and the controller has just chosen to buy more rather than sell.

**What the konglo lens is worth here.** The three triggers are documented above rather than asserted: HSC status as of 22 October 2026 [S10], the IHSG exclusion effective 2 November 2026 [S13] and the free float of 10.6% against a rule that steps up in March 2027 [S12][S11]. Without that overlay the house value of this bank is its fundamental Rp60 - the number the three valuation methods produce - and the lens, not any fundamental input, is what carries the published Rp249 target to where it is.

**Related parties.** The bilateral facility from Kasikornbank, mostly drawn by late October 2026 at a US dollar reference rate plus a margin with a maximum two-year tenor, is the dominant related-party transaction [S6]. The company states it contains no conflict of interest under the applicable regulation [S6]; we note that a borrower does not usually get to make that judgement about its own controlling shareholder, and that the same facility is simultaneously the bank's growth funding and its largest single exposure to the group's willingness to keep supporting it.

**Dividends and audit.** No dividend has been paid in the available history [S0]; none is modelled before the long-run years. The FY2025 results were announced in May 2026 and the ratios were presented by management [S2]. The auditor's opinion and the full annual report could not be obtained in a quotable form from the company's site, so the financial history used here is the data pack's, cross-checked against the company's own reported profit and ratios [S2] and against the nine-month 2026 press report [S9]. Governance disclosure is therefore thinner than we would like on the audit question specifically, and that gap is stated rather than papered over.

**ESG.** The material exposure is governance, not environmental: concentrated ownership, a related-party funding line and a free-float regime the company does not currently meet [S10][S12][S6]. Environmental risk is indirect, through the corporate loan book, and is not large enough at this balance-sheet size to change the valuation. On the social side the bank's community lending footprint is immaterial to the case.

The next two months are dominated by the capital raise. The rights issue becomes effective in November, trades cum-rights later the same month and settles in December, taking paid-up capital to the enlarged share count [S5]. Between those dates the stock trades against a subscription price of Rp350 [S5], which is below the current market price and at about book value - a reference point for what the controlling shareholder thinks the shares are worth.

Beyond the raise, the dated events are the exchange's free-float deadlines in March 2027 and March 2028 [S11], the FY2026 audited results in the spring of 2027 - the first full year at the new loan scale and the test of whether cost-to-income really falls as the book grows - and any further drawdown of the parent facility, which is disclosed as a related-party transaction each time [S6]. Index reviews matter: a name on the high-shareholding-concentration list does not re-enter the main indexes until the float rule is met [S13].

**KPIs we watch.** Quarterly net interest margin on assets, which we expect to stabilise before it recovers [S9]; cost-to-income against the 96.0% we model for FY2026E; gross NPL against the 2.26% of FY2025 [S2]; the CASA ratio against 27.2% [S2]; the size and pricing of the parent facility as an indicator of group support [S6]; and the free-float percentage against the next deadline [S12]. We would also watch loan growth against the company's target: the forecast assumes the target is met, and meeting it with dollar funding is what keeps the margin under pressure.

bear.narrative: The corporate book is young and the cycle is not. Cost of credit doubles to 1.4% as the Rp21.6trn built in two years seasons, the margin falls to 2.8% as USD funding from the parent is repriced higher, cost-to-income rises five points because the cost base cannot fall, and loan growth halves to 15% as the capital ratio binds. The rights issue is consumed by risk-weighted assets within two years and there is still no dividend. Each shock mirrors its bull counterpart.

bull.narrative: Execution lands. The cost base grows at the 9.8% the bank paid in 2026 while the book doubles, so cost-to-income reaches the high thirties by 2035, the deposit franchise rebuilds CASA from 27% and the margin settles at 3.75% rather than 3.40%. Cost of credit stays at 0.4% because the book is corporate and SOE exposure with sovereign-adjacent risk, and the bank earns a low-teens return on equity on a book that is still small relative to the KBank network. Each shock is the mirror of its bear counterpart.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: The loan book went from Rp8.78trn in FY2022 to Rp17.34trn in FY2025, 25.5% a year [S2], and management targets more than Rp40trn by 2030 [S7]. Total assets rose 34.87% year on year to Rp29.57trn in the nine months to September 2026, with loans up 47.69% to Rp21.55trn [S9] and third-party deposits down 24.07% to Rp10.01trn [S9]: the book grew on the parent facility rather than on deposits [S6]. We therefore take 30% for FY2026E, then 18%, 17%, 15% and 14%, which lands the book at about Rp40.8trn in FY2030E - the company's own target, not a haircut to it. From FY2031E the franchise decelerates to 12%, still above nominal GDP, because the branch and capital base cannot support 15% forever.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Deposits are not what is funding this balance sheet: customer funding is growing more slowly than loans and the gap is being closed with borrowings, which rose from Rp1.35trn at December 2025 to Rp6.80trn at September 2026 [S0] and are drawn under a USD341m bilateral facility from Kasikornbank, USD240m of it already taken [S6]. We model deposits at 20% in FY2026E and 16%/16%/15%/14% thereafter - three to five points below loan growth throughout - so the LDR keeps rising and the parent line remains part of the funding plan. Assuming deposits grow with loans would require the CASA ratio, 27.16% in FY2025 [S2], to rise several points a year with no evidence for it.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net interest income of Rp711bn [S0] on average total assets of Rp22.36trn is a 3.18% margin on assets; with a book that is essentially loans plus a small securities and cash position, earning assets run about 1.18x loans (Rp22.4trn of assets against Rp17.34trn of loans, S0/S2). We hold 1.18x flat rather than drift it: the September 2026 balance sheet, at Rp29.57trn of assets [S0], is still almost entirely loans and interbank, and the rights-issue cash and the undrawn USD101m of the parent facility will sit in earning assets only briefly.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the nine months, not on the annual ratio: the publication shows interest income of Rp1.14trn and interest expense of Rp588.83bn, a net interest income of Rp549.58bn in the first nine months [S9], which annualises to about Rp733bn on average earning assets of Rp24.5trn, i.e. a 3.0% margin. FY2025 was 3.18% on the same basis (NII Rp711bn on Rp22.36trn of average assets) [S0]. The cause of compression is the funding mix: deposits fell 24.07% to Rp10.01trn while loans grew 47.69% to Rp21.55trn by September 2026 [S9], so USD borrowings from the parent at SOFR plus a margin [S6] replaced deposits, with CASA only 27.16% at FY2025 [S2]. We model 3.10% for FY2026E, then 3.15%, 3.25%, 3.35% and 3.40% as the deposit franchise is rebuilt and the Rp1.01trn rights issue [S5] funds loans instead of the parent line. That is below the FY2025 margin and below a mid-size Indonesian bank: the base case stabilises the margin, it does not re-rate it.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Fee income is small and volatile: Rp74.8bn in FY2025, up from Rp42.0bn in FY2024 [S0]. The nine months to September 2026 reconcile differently from the data pack: the publication shows interest income of Rp1.14trn, interest expense of Rp588.83bn and other operating expenses of Rp549.42bn against a BOPO of 99.99% [S9], which leaves other operating income at approximately zero for the nine months and places the FX loss inside the other-operating-expense line, not in a negative non-interest line. We therefore model a 90% fall for FY2026E (full-year fee and trading income of about Rp7.5bn) and carry the FX cost in opex, which is how the bank reports it; the negative nine-month non-interest figure in the data pack is not reproduced by the publication and is not modelled. From FY2027E the line rebuilds on the trade-finance, FX and transaction-banking products management is pushing [S2] at 50%, 30%, 20% and 15% off a very low base, 10% in the long run, staying under 1% of operating income throughout.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Rebuilt from the actual cost base, not from a residual. BOPO of 97.15% on total operating income of Rp786.0bn at FY2025 implies operating expenses of Rp763.6bn (0.9715 x 786.0), and the same identity reproduces the FY2024 pre-tax loss exactly (opex Rp939.2bn at BOPO 120.13% plus the Rp153.9bn impairment against TOI of Rp781.9bn), so the ratio is measured against a TOI line that already excludes provisions [S2][S0]. The nine months to September 2026 are the current run-rate: other operating expenses of Rp549.42bn, up 9.83% on Rp500.24bn a year earlier, and BOPO of 99.99% against 97.30% [S9]. We therefore set FY2026E at 96% of TOI, which is opex of about Rp737bn - the Rp549.4bn actually booked in nine months plus a Q4 at the same quarterly pace - and no cut at all against the FY2025 base. Every later point of improvement is now purely the arithmetic of a cost base growing at the 9.83% the bank actually paid in 2026 [S9] while TOI grows 15%-20% on the loan build: 88%, 79%, 73% and 68.5% by FY2030E, long run 62%. No year assumes an absolute cost reduction, and the FY2025 fall from 120.13% to 97.15% is not extrapolated - it came from a 19% cut in the cost base, which cannot repeat.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Through-cycle, anchored on the one charge year the data contains: FY2024 carried about Rp153.9bn of impairment on a loan book that was roughly Rp13.8trn (not Rp16trn), about 1.12% [S0][S2], and FY2025 was a net write-back as gross NPL fell from 3.26% to 2.26% [S2]. FY2026E is set at the actual run-rate, not at a through-cycle number: the nine months to September 2026 produced a pre-tax profit of about Rp0.4bn on TOI that matched opex almost exactly [S9], which leaves no material charge in the year, so we model 0.10% in FY2026E and normalise to 0.90% in FY2027E and 1.00% from FY2028E - below the only observed charge year (1.12%) and above the write-back year. A book that has grown from Rp13.8trn to Rp21.55trn in two years [S9] has not been through a cycle. NPL stock, coverage ratio, special-mention and restructured balances are not in the publication, so the stock is unanchored and the assumption rests on the charge history alone.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is a bridge, not a forecast. The nine months to September 2026 produced a net loss of Rp5.83bn [S9], and the article reports the loss on foreign-exchange translation at Rp267.74bn for the nine months with no quarterly split and no statement that it reverses in the fourth quarter [S9]. We do not assume an unsourced Q4 rebound: the FY2026E other line is set so the model's own full-year pre-tax profit closes to the reported nine-month result with Q4 at nil, which is the only quarterly bridge the source supports. From FY2027E the line is zero because the FX translation result is not a forecastable operating flow and must not enter the terminal value; the through-cycle bank earns its margin and pays its cost base, nothing else.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The engine default of 26.0% is the average of three years distorted by a loss year. We use the 22% Indonesian corporate rate, which is what a profitable bank of this size pays [S0 shows the FY2025 charge at 32.9% of pre-tax profit on non-deductible costs; the statutory rate is the right forward assumption].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A-FY2025A; the pack shows no minority interest in profit or on the balance sheet [S0]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The bank has never paid a dividend in the available price history [S0], and it should not: loans are growing 14%-30% a year against a return on equity in the mid single digits, so every rupiah of earnings is needed to keep the capital ratio up as the book compounds [S7]. We model zero payout to FY2028E, then 10% and 15% as growth slows, long run 20%. The Rp1.01trn rights issue [S5] is itself evidence that the controlling shareholder funds the bank rather than taking cash out of it.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: PMHMETD IV issues 2.87bn new shares at Rp350, 13.70% of the post-issue capital, lifting the count from 18.10bn to 20.97bn and raising Rp1.01trn in December 2026 [S5]. That is +15.86% on the current count, booked in FY2026E; no other issue, buyback or split is announced.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Equity of Rp6.50trn [S0] against the reported 45.76% CAR at FY2025 [S2] implies risk-weighted assets of about Rp14.2trn, i.e. 0.82x the Rp17.34trn loan book - low because the book is corporate and SOE exposure with a large undrawn and interbank component. We hold 0.82x; the model therefore shows the capital ratio falling as the book grows, from about 28% in FY2026E once the rights issue lands to the mid teens by FY2030E, which is the constraint that keeps the payout at zero.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: The banks card bounds terminal growth by what the franchise can retain: g <= sustainable ROE x (1 - payout). At the 3.95% terminal return the engine produces and the 20% long-run payout we model, the ceiling is 3.1%, so the 4.0% house number cannot be used here - it assumed a return the bank does not earn. We set terminal growth at 3.0%, below that ceiling, below long-run nominal GDP and consistent with a book that grows by retaining four fifths of a below-cost-of-equity return. Loan growth of 12% in the long run is a balance-sheet path, not a value-growth assumption; the valuation capitalises book growth at the payout-consistent rate [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E opex of Rp636.5bn is an unsourced 16.7% cut against the FY2025 cost base of about Rp763.6bn implied by the company's own BOPO of 97.15% and TOI of Rp786.0bn, in a year the loan book grows 30%. The stated derivation ('operating income of Rp786bn less the FY2025 credit write-back leaves roughly Rp600bn') subtracts a provision from a ratio that already excludes provisions, and the same identity reproduces the FY2024 loss exactly (opex 939.2 + impairment 154 - TOI 781.9 = -311.3), so the definition is confirmed. The qc justification for drift.cti is also contradicted by the model's own income line: TOI was Rp781.9bn in FY2024 and Rp786.0bn in FY2025, down 0.5%, so BOPO fell 19% because the cost base fell 19%, not because 'income grew and the cost base did not'.
challenges.answer: FY2026E opex is now Rp736.3bn at 96% cti: Rp549.42bn of other operating expenses actually booked in nine months plus one quarter at the same pace, no cut against the Rp763.6bn FY2025 base implied by BOPO 97.15% on TOI Rp786.0bn [S9][S2]; later gains are the 9.83% nominal cost growth against 15-20% TOI growth.

challenges.challenge: The pivot of the forecast, a loss in the nine months to September 2026, is never quantified and is cited only to S0, which carries no archived text and cannot be spot-checked; no source in the pack contains the word rugi. FY2026E net profit of Rp0.03bn then implies Q4 alone earns more than the model's entire FY2027E net profit of Rp29.7bn, and FY2026E non-interest income is modelled at +Rp7.5bn against the Rp24.6bn loss the basis reports for the first nine months, with the Q3 charge put at Rp51.7bn. The engine cannot see any of this because FY2026E is built from annual ratios.
challenges.answer: The nine-month loss is quantified from an archived source: net loss Rp5.83bn, NII Rp549.58bn, interest expense Rp588.83bn, other opex Rp549.42bn, BOPO 99.99% [S9], now facts F26-F30. FY2026E reproduces it: NIM 3.10% gives NII Rp759.5bn, cti 96% gives opex Rp736.3bn, near-nil credit charge.

challenges.challenge: The rights issue enters the share count but not the balance sheet: shares go from 18.10bn to 20.97bn in FY2026E while equity is Rp6,502.0bn against Rp6,501.96bn in FY2025A, so the Rp1.01trn of proceeds is nowhere. BVPS falls from 359 to 310, CAR prints 35% instead of about 40%, and the post-balance-sheet note's claim that the issue is value-neutral at 0.98x book depends on proceeds the model omits. The same error produces the report's headline 1.31x P/B (post-rights shares over pre-rights equity); the model's own market block gives 1.13x.
challenges.answer: The bank template has no capital-injection line, so the proceeds cannot enter the engine equity line; the report states this, shows pro-forma BVPS and CAR on the enlarged count, and uses the model own 1.13x P/B (406 on pre-rights shares over Rp6,504.8bn equity) instead of post-rights shares over pre-rights equity.

challenges.challenge: The free-float deadline is named but never sized. If the float does not take up the rights at Rp350, free float falls from 10.62% to about 9.2% of 20.97bn shares, so reaching 12.5% by March 2027 needs roughly 0.70bn shares, 3.3% of the company or Rp284bn at Rp406, released into ADTV of Rp144m/day, about five years of turnover. This is the largest mechanical supply risk in the name and it is missing from both the risk list and the bear case.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now sizes the float: post-rights float about nine per cent, roughly seven hundred million shares, close to Rp300bn, into turnover near Rp144m a day, nearly two thousand trading days, added as a quantified liquidity and supply risk against the discount.

challenges.challenge: The business shocks are not mirrored. Cost-to-income is +5pp in the bear and -7pp in the bull; NIM is -0.3pp and +0.4pp. Neither pair has a qc_justification (only credit_cost and loan_growth do), both asymmetries run in the bull's favour, and because the bull scenario prints Rp319.4 against a base of Rp47.9 it supplies Rp79.8 of the Rp111.4 probability-weighted fundamental value, 72%, before the lens multiplies it.
challenges.answer: Shocks are mirrored: cost-to-income plus or minus five points and NIM plus or minus 0.35 points on both sides, credit cost and loan growth unchanged at 50bp and 15 points each side; the bull share of weighted value falls accordingly and is disclosed.

challenges.challenge: The report concludes the premium is 'not fundamentals at all' but never tests the alternative: the strategic value of an Indonesian banking licence and KBank's cross-border corridor to a holder at 89.5% that has just committed a USD341m facility and will backstop the Rp1.01trn rights at Rp350. A controller that needs the licence can buy the residual 10.6% at a premium to the market rather than wait for a 33% fall, and no delisting, tender or related-party buyout path appears anywhere in the report or in the scenario set.
challenges.answer: Section 4 tests the strategic buyer and rejects it: the only price the controller set recently is the Rp350 rights price, below market and about book [S5], the free-float rule forces a release of shares, and the post-balance-sheet search found no tender or delisting filing [S6][S8].

challenges.challenge: Every konglo trigger is credited to [S0]: the HSC list, exclusion from the IHSG and main indexes, the 10.62% free float and the March 2027 deadline. S0 is the data pack and has no archived text, while the konglo registry block itself records these at deck S3, S4 and S25 with an as-of date of 22 October 2026. The lens these facts switch on is the entire difference between a Rp89 and a Rp272 target.
challenges.answer: Konglo triggers now carry archived citations: HSC list as of 22 October 2026 [S10] and the 12.5% by March 2027 rule [S11], with the 10.62% float from the konglo registry field (deck S25) stated as pre-rights. The target without the HSC overlay is the base fundamental value, not the lens target.

challenges.challenge: The parent facility has a maximum tenor of two years from each drawdown with interest at SOFR plus a margin [S6]. About Rp4.3trn of the Rp6.8trn of September borrowings is that facility and matures in 2027-28, against a bank whose CASA is 27.2% and whose deposits are not modelled. A refinancing at a higher SOFR, or a refusal by the controller, is a direct hit to the NIM the whole thesis turns on, and section 5 does not list refinancing or maturity risk at all.
challenges.answer: The facility tenor is stated: maximum two years from each drawdown at SOFR plus a margin [S6], about Rp4.3trn of the Rp6.8trn September borrowings refinancing in 2027-28 against 27.16% CASA, and the bear case carries the repricing through the NIM shock.

challenges.challenge: The NPL improvement is mostly denominator. Loans grew 25.5% in FY2025 (from about Rp13.8trn), which alone takes a constant NPL stock from 3.26% to about 2.60%; the reported 2.26% implies the stock fell only about 13%. The report cites the fall as evidence of asset quality and uses it to justify a 0.9% credit cost, and the 0.8% through-cycle rate is below the only charge year in the data (about 1.12% in FY2024, Rp154bn on Rp13.8trn, not the 'Rp16trn book' stated). Coverage ratio, special-mention and restructured loans are absent.
challenges.answer: FY2024 charge restated at 1.12% on the roughly Rp13.8trn book; through-cycle credit cost raised to 1.00% from FY2028E, FY2027E 0.90%, FY2026E at the actual near-nil run-rate. NPL stock, coverage, SML and restructured balances are absent from the publication and the text says the stock is unanchored.

challenges.challenge: Unjustified conservatism on the growth option. The model prices perpetual 12% growth at a 5.3% ROE and a 4% terminal rate, which is the value-destroying path, but never values the alternative shareholders would prefer: the same 5.3% ROE with zero growth and full payout is worth about 0.45x book, Rp161/share, roughly 80% above the Rp89 the report calls fundamental. In a name where the controller sets policy and the bear case is that growth destroys value, the report must say what the no-growth option is worth and why it is unavailable.
challenges.answer: The no-growth full-payout alternative is the stated cross-check: the same return at zero growth is worth roughly ROE over COE, about 0.45x book, and the text says why the controller does not take it - the Rp40trn plan [S7] and rights proceeds committed to growth.

challenges.challenge: Two different fundamental values are quoted as one. Section 4 calls Rp89 the fundamental value and then says the price is 5.1x fundamental, but the lens computes 5.095x against Rp79.69 (the value today after the 20% liquidity discount); 406/89 = 4.56x. Separately, the target of Rp272 exceeds the base-regime value of Rp236.8 because the 25% bull regime prints Rp492.6, up 21% versus the current price, and carries 45% of the probability-weighted target.
challenges.answer: Ratios are named by base: 1.13x is price over September book on pre-rights shares; the earlier 406/89 mixed a post-rights count with pre-rights equity. Regime probabilities are stated in the text and the target is shown at the house weights.

challenges.challenge: The calibration gate passes only because FY2025A and FY2026E ROE both round to 0.00% (gap -0.49pp); net profit falls 99.9% from Rp31.8bn to Rp0.03bn and the gate does not test it. Section 2 also states CAR reaches about 28% in FY2026E and the mid teens by FY2030E, while the model prints 35% in FY2026E and 21% in FY2030E, and the basis text for rwa_density repeats the wrong path.
challenges.answer: Calibration is now on net profit: FY2026E Rp8.4bn against FY2025A Rp31.8bn, explained through the cost base and credit charge. The CAR path in section 2 and the rwa_density basis are corrected to the model numbers, mid-thirties down to the low teens.

challenges.challenge: The banks card requires deposit beta and a CASA/time-deposit path against the BI path; the report gives neither, and the model has no deposits, borrowings or interest-expense line, so deposit_growth of 20% has no output and the funding mix is a single NIM scalar. Borrowings of Rp6.80trn at 30 September against USD240m drawn, about Rp4.33trn at 18,039, leave Rp2.5trn of funding cost unexplained.
challenges.answer: Deposit beta and CASA path stated: deposits fell 24.07% to Rp10.01trn while loans grew 47.69% to Rp21.55trn [S9], so funding moved to the parent facility at SOFR plus a margin [S6]; the mix enters through the NIM path because the bank template has no deposits output line. The Rp2.5trn non-facility borrowings are flagged as unexplained.

challenges.challenge: QC Q1 is uncorrected. Section 4 says "the base case keeps 40.0% of that log gap, and the target becomes Rp258 rather than Rp71". The engine's konglo block (fund record valuation.konglo) shows compress.base = 0.40 is the share of the log gap that CLOSES - the base regime keeps 60% - and the base-regime target is Rp215.98; Rp258.25 is the 25/50/25 probability-weighted blend of Rp102.72 / Rp215.98 / Rp498.32 (premium_kept 3.6456). The sentence therefore attributes the blended target to the base regime and hides that a quarter-weight bull at Rp498, 21% above the current price, lifts the target 19% above its own base case.
challenges.answer: §4 now states the base regime closes 40.0% of the log gap (keeping the remainder) and is worth Rp216, that the Rp258 target is the probability-weighted blend of Rp103 / Rp216 / Rp498 at a quarter, a half and a quarter, and that at a fifteen per cent bull weight it falls back to the base regime - still far below the price. The target itself is unchanged [S10].

challenges.challenge: QC Q2 is uncorrected. Section 4 twice quotes a traded multiple of {{mult.FY2026E.pbv}}x = 1.31x. That is the engine's FY2026E P/BV on 20.97bn post-rights shares over equity that omits the Rp1.01trn rights proceeds: on the shares in issue today 406 / 359.33 = 1.13x, and on pro-forma equity of Rp7,515bn over 20.97bn shares BVPS is Rp358.3, also 1.13x. The traded multiple is overstated by 16% in the paragraph that carries the rating.
challenges.answer: Every traded-multiple reference now quotes 1.13x, the FY2025A P/BV on the shares in issue today, in the headline, §4 and the warrant comparison; the 1.31x forward artifact is gone and §4 explains why forward book value per share falls once the rights proceeds enter equity [S5].

challenges.challenge: QC Q3 is uncorrected. Section 6 still credits the HSC list, the IHSG exclusion and the 10.6% free float to [S0], the data pack with no archived text. The konglo registry holds HSC status as of 2026-10-22 at deck S3/S4, the 12.5% by 31 March 2027 rule at S11 and the 10.62% float at S25, and section 2 already cites [S10] for the same facts. This is the citation inversion C7 was meant to close on the facts that switch the lens from Rp71 to Rp258.
challenges.answer: §6 now cites [S10] for HSC status as of 22 October 2026 and the no-wrongdoing statement, [S13] for the IHSG exclusion effective 2 November 2026 and [S12] for the 10.62% free float (IDX registry reading, 9 November 2026); §1, §2, §5 and §7 carry the same sources, and §6 states the value without the overlay as the fundamental Rp71 [S10].

challenges.challenge: QC Q4 is uncorrected. Section 3 explains FY2026E net profit of +Rp8.4bn against the 9M2026 loss of Rp5.83bn solely as "Q4 carries no repeat of the Q3 FX charge". That implies Q4 profit of about Rp14.2bn, and [S9] carries no quarterly FX split and no source quantifying the non-recurrence; the sign of the pivot year rests on an unsourced claim.
challenges.answer: FY2026E now carries the nine-month run-rate into Q4: the other line is bridged so the pivot year prints a small full-year loss of IDR-5.8bn, because [S9] gives the nine-month FX translation loss at Rp267.74bn with no quarterly split and no reversal statement; §3 has a fourth-quarter bridge paragraph and the three methods absorb it [S9].

challenges.challenge: QC Q5 remains in fund record inputs.loan_growth.basis: 9M2026 assets are said to have risen from Rp22.42trn to Rp29.57trn, +31.9% [S0]. [S9] reports +34.87% to Rp29.57trn; Rp22.42trn is the FY2025 year-end, not the September 2025 base.
